issues.issue: The exclusion bars claims brought "by a Named Insured ... against any other Named Insured," a class that the Additional Named Insureds endorsement (c094) and Endorsements Nos. 6-8 (c123-c126) expand well beyond Item 1, while the next paragraph (c066) switches to the wider word "insured." Whose suit against whom is excluded depends on which term is used.

The exception operates only "if this policy applies to professional liability," but the Professional Services Excluded endorsement (c090) removes professional health care services from the policy and the Contingent Excess Medical Malpractice endorsement (c106) removes medical malpractice for statutory health care providers. Whether the condition in this sentence is ever satisfied can only be answered from those other endorsements.

"[I]ntrafamily liability coverage in cases of automobile liability" has no evident application to a corporate hospital named insured, and the policy nowhere defines intrafamily liability coverage. The sentence's operative scope is indeterminate.

This Wisconsin provision restates cancellation by the named insured in terms that overlap the base policy's Condition 12 (c061) without saying that it replaces it, and it omits c061's rule for multiple named insureds. Which cancellation mechanism the insured must follow is left to construction.

Ten days' notice for cancellation of a policy in force less than 60 days cannot be squared with General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c098), which requires sixty days' written notice "in the event of cancellation or non-renewal." A court would have to decide which endorsement controls.

Cancellation for non-payment on ten days' notice conflicts with General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c098), which requires sixty days' written notice of any cancellation. The Pay Plan endorsement (c103-c104) makes the non-payment trigger a live one.

Mid-term cancellation on ten days' notice conflicts with the sixty-day notice required by General Amendatory Endorsement No. 3 (c098) and with the thirty days stated in Condition 12 (c061). The permissible grounds and the notice period come from different provisions that do not agree.

The paragraph reserves rights "in addition to" those in paragraphs (b) and (c) while omitting paragraph (a), and it applies only to policies without a fixed expiration or longer than one year, which this one-year policy (c004) is not. Whether it has any operation here is a question of its own words.

The insured's right of renewal is on "the terms then being applied by the Company to similar risks," a standard with no defined benchmark for what risks are similar or what terms then apply. The sentence also creates a renewal right the base policy nowhere contemplates.

Making "full compliance by the insured with all the terms of this policy" a condition precedent to any action cannot be squared with the next sentence of the same endorsement (c075), which entitles "any person or organization" to recover to the extent of the insurance afforded, nor with the Wisconsin Declarations provision (c080) limiting the effect of breached conditions. Whether a breach bars suit is contested between them.

This sentence lets "any person or organization or the legal representative thereof" recover under the policy, which sits badly with the condition precedent of full compliance in c074 and with the deleted no-privity rule of Condition 6 (c055). A third-party claimant's direct right of recovery is the point in issue.

"The company will be entitled to a recovery only after the insured has been fully compensated for damages" reverses the apportionment order in the subrogation condition it amends (c059), which reimburses interests paying above the retained limit and then the company. The two priority schemes cannot both be applied to one recovery.

Imputing an agent's knowledge to the company and barring avoidance on that ground contradicts Condition 11 Changes (c060), under which notice to or knowledge of any agent effects no waiver and does not estop the company. Which rule governs an agent's knowledge of a breached condition is a direct conflict.

This provision preserves the company's obligations despite misrepresentation or breach of affirmative warranty unless material or relied on, while Maintenance of Underlying Insurance (c062) is framed as a warranty by the insured with its own stated consequence. Which regime governs a failure of the underlying-insurance warranty must be worked out between them.

The rule that no failure of a condition prior to loss affects the company's obligation unless it increases the risk or contributes to the loss is irreconcilable with the Action Against Company endorsement (c074), which makes full compliance with all terms a condition precedent to suit. Late notice under c050 would put the two squarely against each other.

The exclusion reaches acts or omissions "of any insured subject of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 ... with respect to their duties under pension or Employee benefit plans," a garbled phrase that does not say whether the insured or the liability must be subject to ERISA. Its reach over an employee-benefits claim is therefore uncertain.

Limb (b) excludes property damage to any property merely "used by any Insured hereunder," a boundless category that, once General Amendatory Endorsement No. 1 (c096) makes lessors of premises and equipment insureds, would exclude damage to virtually every premises and item of equipment the hospital occupies. The scope of "used by" and "any Insured" is what a court would have to construe.

"[D]irectors and officers are excluded from this contract for liability arising out of 'wrongful acts'" is ambiguous as to whether it excludes those persons as insureds or merely excludes wrongful-act liability. The distinction decides whether a director is covered for anything at all.

"Wrongful Acts" is defined by reference to directors or officers "of the company," but "company" throughout this policy means the insurer (see c008-c016), not the named insured. Read literally, the definition catches no one connected with the hospital.

The exception restores liability arising out of personal injury, bodily injury, property damage, hospital professional liability and advertisers liability, which is substantially everything the insuring agreement (c009) covers, leaving the Directors and Officers exclusion (c084) with little or nothing to operate on. Whether the exclusion retains any content is a whole-instrument question.

This endorsement removes all discrimination injury from "personal injury," while the policy definition (c034)(5) expressly includes racial or religious discrimination not committed by or on behalf of the insured, except where prohibited by law. The two cannot both be given effect on a discrimination claim.

The exclusion reaches injury "at any time of the manufacture of, or mining of, or use of, or exposure to Asbestos products," wording that does not say whether ordinary occupancy of an asbestos-containing building is "use of" asbestos products. Its boundary as against a premises claim is undefined.

Withdrawing the duty to defend any asbestos suit conflicts with the Supplementary Payments obligation (c010), under which the company "shall defend any suit ... even if such suit is groundless, false or fraudulent" where no underlying coverage applies. Which governs a mixed asbestos and non-asbestos suit is unresolved.

The wholesale exclusion of professional health care services cannot be squared with the Aggregate Limits Endorsement (c093), which fixes an aggregate for loss "arising out of ... any professional liability hazard," nor with the Contingent Excess endorsement (c110), which disapplies this form in stated circumstances. Whether the policy affords any professional liability cover is decided among these provisions.

The exception turns entirely on which "entities or individuals" are "not subject to the Wisconsin Patients Compensation Fund," a status the policy neither defines nor lists for the many named and additional insureds. Coverage for a given insured's professional services cannot be determined from the endorsement's own words.

This amended Limit of Liability again imports "the amount stated in Item 3 of the declarations," which General Amendatory Endorsement No. 4 (c118) purports to change while calling it Item 2, and which the declarations state as $18,000,000. The controlling each-occurrence figure is contested between them.

The aggregate is extended to loss arising out of "any professional liability hazard," a term the policy nowhere defines, unlike the defined products and completed operations hazards (c042, c043) it sits beside. Whether hospital malpractice loss is aggregated, and on what footing, depends on that undefined phrase.

The statement that "no automatic coverage for entities newly acquired by any of them is extended hereby" cannot be squared with the Named Insured definition (c028), which automatically includes any subsidiary and any organization under the named insured's control. Whether an unlisted affiliate is insured turns on which provision controls.

Additional insured status is granted "only with respect to their interest in the operations of the Named Insured," a limitation given no content beyond the one-line "insurable interest" entries such as "As their interest may appear." What liability of a lessor, lender or university is within its "interest in the operations" is left open.

Sixty days' written notice on any cancellation or non-renewal contradicts the ten-day periods in the Cancellation - Wisconsin endorsement (c069-c071) and the thirty days in Condition 12 (c061). Which notice period a cancellation must satisfy is a direct conflict of provisions.

The endorsement replaces "the exclusion relating to the discharge, dispersal, release or escape of smoke, vapors ... or pollutants," but the exclusion it describes (c030) is worded differently and carries a sudden-and-accidental exception this form drops. Identifying what was replaced, and whether anything of c030 survives, requires reading the two together.

"Pollutants" is defined as any solid, liquid, gaseous or thermal "irritant or contaminant," a phrase with no stated boundary that on its face would capture ordinary hospital substances such as medical gases, cleaning agents and medical waste. The general words are given content only by the illustrative list they follow.

The schedule lists an "Initial 25% Deposit" of $7,470 plus ten further installments, but labels the last of them the "Eleventh Installment" and carries an impossible due date ("42/04/1996"). The number and timing of required payments cannot be read off the table as printed.

The sentence declares payments "past due" but attaches no consequence to that status — no interest, no grace period, no forfeiture. Its only operation must be imported from the non-payment cancellation provision (c070), which it does not mention.

The exclusion on its face applies to "the Insured" generally, while General Amendatory Endorsement No. 2 (c097) attaches this form "only as respects Med-Health Financial Services." Whether collection-agency activity by any other insured is excluded depends on reading the two together.

The exclusion of medical malpractice cover for "any entity which is defined by Wisconsin Statute, Section 655.001 as a health care provider" imports a statutory definition without saying which of the many named and additional insureds meets it. The endorsement's reach cannot be fixed from its own terms.

Extending the statutory definition of "health care provider" to "subsidiaries of holding companies of the named insured" is ambiguous as to whether it captures affiliates of the named insured itself, and it conflicts with the Named Insured definition (c028) which already sweeps subsidiaries in as insureds. Which entities lose malpractice cover is what the phrase decides.

The contingent cover applies "directly over the underlying insurance listed in this policy and identified as being listed for contingency coverage purposes," but the Schedule of Underlying Insurance (c007) identifies no policy as listed for that purpose. The attachment point of the contingent cover has no referent in the instrument.

The company "at its sole option may make an appropriate premium charge" which the named insured agrees to pay, without any standard for what is appropriate or any cap. The insured's obligation is fixed unilaterally by an undefined term.

This sentence disapplies "Form No. 035(12/87) Professional Services Excluded," but the form actually attached to the policy is Form No. 035 WI (1/94) (c090-c091). Whether the disapplication reaches the form in the policy is a question of matching this endorsement to that one.

The endorsement amends "the Policy Territory provisions of the Hospital Professional Liability coverage part attached to the policy," but no such coverage part is attached to this umbrella policy, whose territory clause is c018. It also duplicates, in an earlier statutory version, the endorsement at c119.

This recital of the fund-recovery condition differs from the later version in c120-c121, which adds the requirement that the provider or employee "has coverage under the fund." Two inconsistent recitations of the same statute sit in the same policy.
This extension-of-time sentence is duplicated verbatim at c122 as part of a differently worded recital of the same statute. Which recital the policy incorporates is left open.

The promise to indemnify the Named Insured for legal expenses of resolving an inter-insurer dispute sits against the definition of ultimate net loss (c032), which excludes all loss and legal expenses, and against Other Insurance (c058), which fixes how this policy shares with others. Whether these expenses are payable, and on top of what limit, must be worked out among the three.

This Trebled Damages Exclusion is Form 009-133, which General Amendatory Endorsement No. 5 in the policy deletes and declares "null and void," yet the form remains in the assembled instrument. Whether the exclusion is part of the policy is the question.

The promise to pay one-third of the total trebled sum cannot be squared with the preceding sentence (c115), which limits coverage to actual compensatory damages and says the policy "shall not apply to trebled damages." One paragraph excludes what the next pays.

Defining "damages" to exclude plaintiff's legal fees only "[f]or purposes of this exclusion" leaves a second, narrower meaning of a term used throughout the insuring agreement (c009) and the ultimate net loss definition (c032). Which meaning applies to an antitrust judgment including fees is open.

The endorsement amends "the policy limits in Item 2," but Item 2 of the declarations is the Policy Period; the limits appear in Item 3, and the consideration line for additional premium is left blank. On its face the amendment operates on the wrong item and for no stated consideration.

The $20,000,000 each occurrence and $20,000,000 aggregate stated here contradict the $18,000,000 each occurrence and $9,000,000 aggregate in the declarations (c005), which the Limit of Liability clauses (c016, c092) incorporate by reference. Which figures cap the company's liability is a direct conflict.

Like c111, this endorsement amends "the Policy Territory provisions of the Hospital Professional Liability coverage part attached to the policy," which does not exist in this umbrella policy whose territory clause is c018. It also duplicates c111 in a different statutory text, both of which remain in the assembled policy.

This condition of recovery from the fund differs from the earlier recital at c112, which omits the requirement that the provider have coverage under the fund. The policy carries two inconsistent versions of the same amendment.

This notice alternative conflicts with the corresponding sentence in the earlier Policy Territory endorsement (c112), which requires only that the fund be notified within 60 days without the coverage-under-the-fund condition. Which version governs an out-of-state action is unresolved.

This extension-of-time sentence repeats c113 word for word as part of a competing recital of Wis. Stat. 655.27(5)(a)2. The duplication leaves it unclear which endorsement's text the policy incorporates.

The endorsement says it is effective on the policy's inception date "unless otherwise stated herein" while carrying a stated effective date of 07/08/1996, and it amends "Form 0098-052" where the schedule and the Additional Named Insureds endorsement (c094) show Form 009-052. The date on which Children's Specialty Group became an insured, and the form amended, are both uncertain.

The endorsement bears an effective date of 01/01/1997 yet states that it is effective on the inception date of the policy unless otherwise stated. Whether CMG - Brown Deer Campus is a Named Insured from 03/01/1996 or only from 01/01/1997 is left ambiguous by these two statements.

This endorsement amends Item 1 to "Children's Health System, Inc.", differing from "Children's Health Systems, Inc." as declared in c001 and used in every other endorsement heading. Which entity is the Named Insured, and whether the change is a correction or a substitution, is the question.

The addition is made to "Form 009-052," the Additional Named Insureds endorsement (c094), which itself denies automatic coverage to newly acquired entities. Whether these campuses are named insureds in their own right or merely divisions of an existing one is left unstated.

This endorsement is headed as attached to and forming part of Policy No. HPP-1996-4104-00, which is the underlying comprehensive general liability policy listed in Item 7 (c007), not this umbrella policy UML-1996-4104-00. Whether the increased $1,000,000/$3,000,000 professional liability limits form part of this contract at all is the issue.

The Company "at its sole option may make an appropriate premium charge" if limits must be increased, with no standard for appropriateness and no statement of who decides that an increase is "required." The obligation to pay is left to unilateral determination.
